extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, producers, WGA members, and participants in WGA credit determinations/arbitrations
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of the Writers Guild of America rules, procedures, and criteria for assigning writing credits on motion pictures and television programs, including forms of credit, contribution thresholds, team rules, notification requirements, evidence submission, and arbitration procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum contribution threshold for credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Since its inception, writers must have contributed at least 33 percent of a final script to receive credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the purposes of arbitration, to be awarded a screenplay credit the writer must have contributed more than 33 percent of the final screenplay. The WGA acknowledges the difficulty in determining such percentages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher threshold for non-original screenplay authors
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of an original screenplay, writers who did not write the original must contribute more than 50 percent to receive the credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule distinguishes original screenplay authors from subsequent contributors; the WGA notes difficulty in precise percentage determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on number of credited writers/teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Up to three writers, or two teams of writers in film and three teams of writers in television, may receive credit for a production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No more than two writers can share a screenplay credit except in cases of arbitration; from arbitration, screenplay credits can be given to either three individual writers or two teams of writers. Teams of writers, regardless of how many people are in them, are considered as one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team definition and team-credit rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A team of writers is 'two writers who have been assigned at about the same time to the same material and who work together for approximately the same length of time on the material'; their work is considered a joint contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A team is credited with an ampersand (&) separating their names. To change a team designation a writer must openly question it at the time the work is submitted to the WGA. If one member of a team is hired as an additional writer, both team writers must agree for the additional writer to take the shared credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit forms and definitions (Written by / Screenplay by / Story by / Teleplay by)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Written by" is for writers who can claim both the story and screenplay/teleplay elements, except when there is 'source material of a story nature'. "Screenplay by" may be used when the writers for the story and screenplay are different. "Story by" is distinct from screenplay/teleplay and consists of basic narrative, idea, theme or outline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen Story by/Television Story by used when work is based on but substantially different from source material. Limits: story credits cannot be shared by more than two writers in film and three in television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source material and source credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials used for research are not credited, but source material as defined by the WGA receives credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate credit wording should indicate the nature/relationship of source material (examples: 'From a Play by', 'From a Novel by', 'Based upon a Story by', 'Based upon a [teleplay/Screenplay] by'). The WGA recommends against using 'Adaptation by' except in special arbitration cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separated rights (Created by / Developed (for Television) by)
rubrics_metrics.description: Television has 'Created by' and 'Developed (for Television) by' credits under a crediting structure known as separated rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers entitled to 'Created by' credits will have developed a significant part of the format, story, and teleplay, and also get sequel rights. 'Created by' credits are given on every episode; 'Developed (for Television) by' credits are only given on episodes the writer explicitly contributed material to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of names in credits
rubrics_metrics.description: In credits, names are usually ordered by who did the most work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the order is disagreed upon and arbitration finds that all writers contributed equally, the names will be ordered chronologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification and notice of tentative credits (MBA requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The production company must supply all participant writers and the Writers Guild a notice of tentative credits, and give all participant writers a copy of either the shooting script or latest revised script, promptly upon the conclusion of photography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All writers on a project have the right to know who else has written on that project. The MBA also requires production to tell new writers who has preceded them; television productions of a motion picture over 90 minutes have a specific written-notice requirement informing writers of those who follow them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timelines to respond to tentative credits
rubrics_metrics.description: There are specified minimum time periods in which tentative credits must remain open for challenge before a production may finalize them (different for film and television under the MBA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For film productions the time cannot be earlier than specified business days (notes cite 7–12 business-day windows depending on emergency clauses); for television different minimums apply (examples cited: 3–7 business days depending on circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to be involved even if deceased
rubrics_metrics.description: Any participant writer, even deceased, has the right to be involved in the credit determination process (this may be through a representative, such as an agent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WGA treats participant writers' involvement as a right; representatives may participate on behalf of deceased writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping and submitting written material as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is vital that the writer keep copies of all work done, and submit copies to the Writers Guild promptly upon completion; scripts as well as substantial story ideas and other literary material are counted for credit decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All participant writers and the production must cooperate by accurately submitting all written material (original and in triplicate) to be considered. The WGA notes that not every draft must be submitted—only material the writer 'deems relevant to demonstrate his/her writing contribution to the final shooting script.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of writers' arbitration statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers are advised to submit a written statement to the arbitration committee outlining their stance and detailing their claim to credit in line with Writers Guild policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements cannot include anything irrelevant to the case, reference to compensation, letters of support from other people, or information on the development that will not help the arbiters in their purely analytical review. Participant writers have 24 hours to give their statements; late statements will be accepted as long as they come before a decision is made. The WGA keeps writers' statements private.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration composition and eligibility of arbiters
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no agreement on writing credits, three members of the Writers Guild are selected as arbiters; they must have no interest in the decision and meet eligibility criteria (film: member for five years or three screen credits; television: member for at least one year and at least three writing credits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At least two selected members must have been on at least two arbitration committees before. The Screen/Television Arbiters List of eligible members is sent to all participant writers who can preclude a reasonable number of names; selection is then made from the remaining names. Arbiters' identities are kept anonymous to everyone except the Screen/Television Credits Committee. A member of the Screen/Television Credits Committee is designated to advise the arbiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration timelines and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Film arbitration takes place over 21 business days, and television arbitration over eight (per the article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbiters receive tentative credits, writers' statements, summary of issues, all written material with a chronological record, a copy of the Screen/Television Credits Manual, and are requested to communicate decisions first by telephone then in writing. If arbiters cannot unanimously agree they teleconference with the advisor and, in absence of unanimity, a majority decision is accepted. A participant writer may request an appeal before an internal Policy Review Board within 24 hours of the arbiters' decision being communicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Policy Review Board appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Policy Review Board only serves to determine if there was any 'serious deviation from the policy of the Guild or the procedure as set forth in [the Screen/Television Credits Manual]' through the process of the arbitration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board does not read submitted written materials nor judge writers' contributions; it may annul an arbitration decision only if policy or procedure was broken, and may ask arbiters to reconsider or order a new arbitration committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reopening arbitration after changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Should the screenplay be rewritten after the final credits decision has been made, arbitration may be reopened within 48 hours of the final changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows credit determinations to respond to substantive changes occurring immediately after a decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling doubts about authenticity (hearings and additional evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In situations where there is doubt over the authenticity of the submitted written material, a hearing may be held before arbitration where the writers provide testimony and evidence as to authorship, sequence, and legitimacy of the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Writers Guild may also request a cutting continuity (film) or an 'as broadcast' script (television) which the production must provide if available; writers may ask the WGA to request this if they believe the final script is not reflective of what was actually filmed. Cutting continuities and as broadcast scripts do not themselves receive a writing credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: WGA presumption about access to prior material
rubrics_metrics.description: The Writers Guild officially presumes that any writer has access to all prior material written for the project during their employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption underscores credits given to prior writers who have been removed from projects and affects how contributions based on prior material are evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on producers/directors receiving writing credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers and directors cannot receive the story/screenplay/teleplay credit unless there are either no other writers for the story/screenplay/teleplay or the decision is taken to arbitration, and the WGA must have been notified of a writing team that includes a producer/director and a non-producer/director at the commencement of the team's work together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents undue credit for production staff except in limited or arbitrated circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special and other credit forms (Special Material by, Narration Written by, Based on Characters Created by, Adaptation by)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other credits may be used for specific situations: 'Narration Written by', 'Based on Characters Created by', 'Adaptation by', and a 'Special Material by' credit for television when material does not qualify for other credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Special Material by' can be given to writers on some forms of television shows and has no limit on how many people may receive it. The WGA provides that 'Adaptation by' should be used only in special arbitration cases and generally recommends against it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on content in arbitration statements (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements to arbitration cannot include irrelevant information such as reference to compensation, letters of support, or development information that will not help arbiters in their analytical review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WGA provides examples of non-useful development info, e.g., 'the fact that a project was greenlit after a certain draft is irrelevant in determining credits'. Irrelevant material may harm the statement's usefulness to arbiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudonym usage and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: A pseudonym may be used if the writer is to be paid less than US$200,000 (for film) or less than three times the applicable minimum in their MBA (for television), if the pseudonymous name is deemed reasonable and if the writer requests this within five business days of the final credits being determined (for film) or within a preset time frame (for television).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before a pseudonym can be used, it must be registered with the Writers Guild. A pseudonym may not duplicate the name or pseudonym of another writer or the name of a public figure. The Writers Guild does not define 'reasonable' in this context. Using a pseudonym does not remove rights to compensation; withdrawing from credit does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal from credit rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer may withdraw from credit 'for personal cause' before the tentative notice is submitted; if the other writers do not agree, it shall be taken to arbitration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A writer cannot withdraw from credit after arbitration. Withdrawing from credit includes losing rights to and compensation from the material; using a pseudonym does not remove these rights.
